intro.text: Oshkosh Corporation is a global industrial technology company that designs and deploys advanced technologies to empower everyday heroes who build, serve and protect communities around the world. Across construction, firefighting, aviation, refuse collection, defense and delivery industries, we create purpose-built vehicles, equipment and integrated ecosystems that are safe, intuitive and highly productive. As an innovator and integrator, we work directly with our customers to solve real-world challenges – developing and applying breakthrough technologies in autonomy, artificial intelligence, connectivity and electrification. Through these advancements, we make some of the world’s toughest jobs safe, efficient, sustainable and connected — delivering measurable impact for the people who depend on us every day.

sbc.text: Net operating costs for corporate and other increased primarily due to the intangible asset impairments in the second quarter of 2024 at Pratt Miller ($52 million), higher share-based compensation expenses ($6 million), lower operating results at Pratt Miller ($6 million) and higher new product development investments ($5 million).

wc.text: The Company continues to actively monitor its liquidity position and working capital needs and prioritizes capital expenditures related to capacity and strategic investments. The Company believes that its liquidity position is adequate to meet its projected needs. To provide additional flexibility for working capital needs, organic and inorganic investments as well as share repurchases, the Company amended the Credit Agreement in April 2024 to increase the maximum aggregate amount of availability under the Revolving Credit Facility by $450 million to $1.55 billion.

capex.text: Oshkosh also continued investing in growth through capital expenditures of $281 million, which included continued investment in the Company's production capabilities at its facilities in Tennessee and South Carolina. The Company also invested $169 million in research and development, an increase of nearly 30% compared to the previous year. Oshkosh believes these investments help to position the Company for long-term success and shareholder value creation.

lines.name: Cash and cash equivalents
lines.why: Cash can repay debt or be paid out: a financial asset. Cash needed to run the business is operating; move it if you know how much.

lines.name: Receivables
lines.why: Owed by customers for sales: operating.

lines.name: Inventory
lines.why: Goods held for sale: operating.

lines.name: Prepaid and other current assets
lines.why: Prepayments and other operating items: operating.

lines.name: Property, plant and equipment
lines.why: Assets used to produce and sell: operating.

lines.name: Operating lease right-of-use assets
lines.why: Leased stores, offices and equipment used in the business: operating.

lines.name: Goodwill
lines.why: Paid for acquired businesses: operating.

lines.name: Intangible assets
lines.why: Acquired technology, brands and customer relationships: operating.

lines.name: Equity-method investments
lines.why: Stakes in associated businesses, usually part of operations. Financial if held as an investment.

lines.name: Deferred tax assets
lines.why: Taxes on operating income paid ahead: operating.

lines.name: Other non-current assets
lines.why: Other long-term operating items: operating.

lines.name: Accounts payable
lines.why: Owed to suppliers for operations: operating.

lines.name: Accrued liabilities
lines.why: Wages, services and other costs not yet paid: operating.

lines.name: Deferred revenue
lines.why: Customers' payments ahead of delivery: operating.

lines.name: Income taxes payable
lines.why: Taxes on operating income: operating.

lines.name: Other current liabilities
lines.why: Other operating items due within a year: operating.

lines.name: Short-term debt and commercial paper
lines.why: Borrowed money: financial.

lines.name: Long-term debt
lines.why: Bonds, notes and loans: financial.

lines.name: Finance lease liabilities
lines.why: Leases that work like a loan for the asset: financial.

lines.name: Operating lease liabilities
lines.why: Rent owed on leases used in the business: operating by default. Move it to financing to treat leases like debt (if the balance sheet has no lease line of its own, they sit inside other liabilities).

lines.name: Deferred tax liabilities
lines.why: Taxes on operating income deferred: operating.

lines.name: Deferred revenue, non-current
lines.why: Customers' payments for later years: operating.

lines.name: Other non-current liabilities
lines.why: Other long-term operating obligations: operating.

lines.name: Other assets, not tagged separately
lines.why: Total assets minus the lines above: assets the company tags its own way. Operating by default.

lines.name: Other liabilities, not tagged separately
lines.why: Total liabilities minus the lines above: liabilities the company tags its own way. Operating by default.

s.t: The Company has three reportable segments: Access, Vocational and Transport, which comprised 43%, 36% and 20%, respectively, of the Company’s 2025 consolidated net sales.
Approximately 18% of our net sales in 2025 were attributable to products sold outside of the United States, of which approximately 47% involved export sales from the United States.
Sales to the U.S. government comprised approximately 20% of the Company’s net sales in 2025.
No other single customer accounted for more than 10% of the Company’s net sales for this period.

International sales comprised approximately 18% of overall net sales in 2025, of which approximately 47% involved exports from the U.S. The majority of export sales in 2025 were denominated in U.S. dollars.
No other customer represented more than 10% of sales.
Through these advancements, we make some of the world’s toughest jobs safe, efficient, sustainable and connected — delivering measurable impact for the people who depend on us every day.
The Company maintains leading market shares across nearly all of its businesses and is the sole-source supplier for several key vehicle platforms to the DoD.

In an effort to be a single-source supplier for its customers, Pierce offers a full line of custom and commercial fire apparatus and emergency vehicles, including pumpers, aerial platforms, ladder and tiller trucks, tankers, light-, medium- and heavy-duty rescue vehicles, wildland rough terrain response vehicles and other emergency response vehicles.

Principal methods of competition include brand awareness, product innovation and performance, price, quality, service and support, product availability and the extent to which a company offers single-source customer solutions.

Principal methods of competition include brand awareness, ability to meet or exceed customer specifications, price, lead times, the extent to which a company offers single-source customer solutions, product innovation, product quality, dealer distribution and service and support.

Competition for DoD programs currently supplied by the Company could result in the U.S. government awarding future contracts to another manufacturer or the U.S. government awarding the contracts to the Company at lower prices and operating margins than the Company experiences under current contracts.
These technologies are evolving and, in many cases, rely on third-party tools, data, software or infrastructure.
The Company generates significant capital resources from operating activities, which is the expected primary source of funding for the Company.
Customers of the Company, from time to time, may fund purchases from the Company through third-party finance companies.
The Company’s ultimate profitability on such contracts may depend on the eventual outcome of an equitable settlement of contractual issues with the Company’s customers.

During a suspension or debarment, the Company would also be prohibited from selling equipment or services to customers that depend on loans or financial commitments from the Export-Import Bank, Overseas Private Investment Corporation and similar U.S. government agencies.
